title: Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016
short_title: Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would add a new goal to aviation and maritime security laws: stopping serious or organised crime at airports, seaports, and offshore oil and gas facilities.
It would change the background check rules for aviation and maritime security identification cards to consider serious criminal offences, not just security threats.
The bill also clarifies the legal basis for background checks and allows regulations to set penalties for offences related to serious or organised crime.
changes: Gives the Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 and the Maritime Transport and Offshore Facilities Security Act 2003 an extra purpose to reduce criminal influence.
Strengthens the eligibility criteria for ASICs and MSICs to target serious criminal offences.
Allows regulations to prescribe penalties for breaking the new serious or organised crime requirements.
Clarifies the legislative basis for background checks under the Maritime Act.
Inserts a severability provision to guide a court on Parliament's intention.
summary.affected: Anyone who must hold an aviation security identification card (ASIC) or a maritime security identification card (MSIC) to access secure zones at airports, seaports, and offshore oil and gas facilities.

I commend the amendments. Fiona Nash The government will not be supporting the proposed amendments from Senator Leyonhjelm. The existing ASIC and MSIC schemes protect against unlawful interference with aviation and maritime transport and offshore facilities. The purpose of the bill is to broaden the ASIC and MSIC schemes to also capture persons convicted of serious or organised crime offences, to improve the government's ability to combat serious or organised crime. Limiting any serious or organised crime offences to a connection with terrorism minimises the improvement to the ASIC and MSIC schemes. It prevents the government from implementing the recommendations of the parliamentary Joint Committee on Law Enforcement and the National Ice Taskforce to address serious or organised crime in the aviation and maritime sectors. speeches.speaker: Darren Chester
speeches.brief: The bill strengthens aviation and maritime security by introducing new eligibility criteria for security identification card schemes, targeting serious or organised crime. It adds offences such as firearms trafficking and foreign incursion to background checks, and shifts focus from minor offences to higher-risk convictions, with organised crime costing Australia $36 billion annually.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The opposition moved an amendment to the Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016, arguing the government’s policies inconsistently toughen background checks on Australian aviation and maritime workers while allowing foreign crews with weaker vetting to replace them, undermining security and Australian jobs. The amendment notes the government’s failure to articulate a policy at the 2016 election, its WorkChoices On Water legislation, the MV Portland case, and calls for urgent development of aviation and maritime policies that prioritise Australian jobs and reliable background checks.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016 would strengthen eligibility criteria for aviation and maritime security identification cards to prevent serious or organised crime, including implementing a National Ice Taskforce recommendation. He also noted a national 8.4% increase in car thefts over the past 12 months, with a 31.4% rise in Victoria and 31% of stolen vehicles never recovered, and highlighted export loopholes for stolen cars.

speeches.speaker: Josh Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016 is unclear, may unfairly discriminate against workers, and leaves major security gaps, while criticising the government’s weakening of Australian coastal shipping and port privatisation—citing Fremantle’s 34.91 million tonnes of trade worth $26.1 billion and nearly $40 billion in state debt.

speeches.speaker: Darren Chester
speeches.brief: The Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016 expands the Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 and Maritime Transport and Offshore Facilities Security Act 2003 to prevent individuals linked to serious or organised crime from accessing airports, seaports, and offshore facilities. It introduces harmonised eligibility criteria for ASIC and MSIC schemes, fulfills a government election commitment and a key action from the National Ice Taskforce response, and was previously introduced on 11 February 2016, passing the House on 16 March 2016 before lapsing.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The speaker moved amendments to replace "serious or organised" with "serious and organised" throughout the Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016, arguing the original wording was broader than recommended by the National Ice Taskforce and the Joint Committee on Law Enforcement. The amendments aim to keep the definition precisely targeting serious and organised crime, particularly drug trafficking, rather than diluting it.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Labor opposed the government's rejection of Senate amendments to the Transport Security Amendment (Serious or Organised Crime) Bill 2016, arguing the government should accept the amendments—moved by Senator Leyonhjelm—to pass the legislation rather than let it fail.
